extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of mass communication, journalism students, media researchers, and media policy analysts
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and evaluate how organizational structures, ownership patterns, and internal control mechanisms shape news and media content. Emphasizes owner policy, corporate ownership changes, chain and cross-ownership effects, newsroom control practices, and workforce adaptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection for organizational marketing/synergy
rubrics_metrics.description: Messages may be selected not for their importance to an audience, their newsworthiness, or their artistic significance, but for how they fit into a larger organizational marketing scheme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: company products featured in company films or magazines when tied to corporate synergy (Time Warner example, Coca-Cola and Columbia Pictures). Concern: stories expected to be affirmative/upbeat and avoid reflecting negatively on company products. Anti-pattern: selecting content primarily to promote corporate products or cross-promote across holdings rather than on newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Owner influence and top-level policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Owners or their appointed top executives have the final say in what the organization does; by establishing policy for the entire organization, media owners have an unmistakable impact on media content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and evidence: owner-imposed cuts and staff changes (Mortimer Zuckerman at NY Daily News), overt editorial interventions (Murdoch's changes at Sun‑Times, use of newspapers to support politicians). Owners can impose views, praise restrictions (Zuckerman on Gulf War), or be criticized for potential editorial power. Mechanisms include direct orders, policy memos, hiring/firing, and setting organizational objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes in corporate ownership alter values, culture, and content
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporate takeovers often bring different values, objectives, and cultures that ultimately change content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 1980s network ownership changes (Tisch/Loews, Capital Cities, GE) led new owners to demand news 'support itself' rather than be a loss-leader. Effect: shifts toward cost-conscious, profit-oriented news decisions and possible content changes (e.g., more sensational or entertainment-oriented coverage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic imperatives shape news mission and style
rubrics_metrics.description: Economic pressures (declining ad revenue, rising costs, debt-to-equity shifts) push organizations to treat news like other businesses, influencing mission and style of news divisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences include pressure to make news divisions self-supporting, increased sensationalism or docudrama-style news, and managerial interventions when stakes are high. Source: critics like Peter Boyer linking sensationalism to economic change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consolidation and conglomerate size leading to homogenization
rubrics_metrics.description: The sheer size and concentration of media conglomerates increases the potential for homogenized content across outlets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: Bagdikian's Media Monopoly findings (decline from ~50 to ~20 corporations controlling most U.S. media). Concern: fewer independent owners and cross-organizational effects among conglomerate holdings that can reduce diversity and distinctiveness of content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal slant: editorial endorsements and invisible bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial endorsements and the editorial voice may influence supposedly 'objective' news pages, producing subtle slants (e.g., in poll coverage) rather than overtly partisan news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings: newspapers often endorse candidates and poll coverage favors endorsed candidates; even non-endorsing papers show bias in reporting polls. Studies show publisher attitude correlates with paper treatment of issues and reporting differences across papers on the same event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple ownership and cross-ownership effects on diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies owning multiple media outlets (including both newspapers and broadcast organizations) can affect the news product and reduce local comprehensiveness and media diversity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: cross-owned markets can have less comprehensive news coverage for individual communities. Cross-ownership may also cause news values to flow from newspaper to television, potentially changing broadcast content. Studies cited (Wirth & Wollert; Wollert; Stempel).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chain versus independent ownership differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Chain ownership (group-owned papers) tends to be more absentee, may weaken community attachments of staff, and can change coverage priorities compared with independently owned papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effects noted: chain papers devote less space to local community conflict, fewer argumentative or local/controversial editorials, more homogenous presidential endorsements across chain members, and socialization of employees to chain-wide roles. Mitigating findings: chains can also bring capital and standardize practices; empirical results mixed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational control mechanisms (how power is exercised)
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations exert control through rewards (promotions, raises), punishments (demotions, firing), formal policy memos, and subtle, unwritten norms that guide daily decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: memos instructing story/photo selection to reflect community values; editorial blue-penciling; rare explicit reprimands serve as signals. Control operates both overtly (policy directives) and covertly (reward/punishment incentives, career advancement tied to conformity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Breed's social control and covert policy maintenance
rubrics_metrics.description: Unwritten policies and a 'consistent orientation' are maintained covertly so that staff conform despite personal disagreements; policy is often enforced by routine practices rather than explicit orders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Breed's mechanisms: reporters learn acceptable norms by observing what kinds of stories pass, blue-penciling and retroactive edits are explained away by time/space pressures, and internal communications reinforce acceptable boundaries. The goal of 'getting the news' can override individual objections to policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-censorship and adaptation by journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters often self-regulate or self-censor to align with organizational interests, striving to be rewarded with scoops, access, bylines, or reputation; those who threaten institutional interests are marginalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: reporters avoid divergence from 'common wisdom' to maintain credibility with editors; killing stories causes subsequent self-censorship. Elbot's 'invisible hand' and examples of reporters who become nonthreatening to dominant culture (Jill Nelson's account) illustrate adaptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workforce diversity constrained by organizational culture
rubrics_metrics.description: A more diverse workforce can improve coverage of minority issues, but minority journalists may be pressured to adapt to dominant organizational norms and thus may have limited ability to change portrayals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings: minority reporters may have stories labeled 'not newsworthy' or dropped for space/time; some successful minority journalists 'refashion' themselves to fit the dominant culture (e.g., writing stories that pathologize their own communities). Organizational socialization can dilute minority perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchy, remoteness, and organizationwide pressures for conformity
rubrics_metrics.description: Remoteness of top editors/executives, bureaucratic layers, and the lack of need to justify decisions reinforce conformity and make subordinates guess what will please superiors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gans: top editors maintain power through these organizationwide pressures; reporters object to edits yet accept editors' authority to kill stories. This dynamic fosters subtle pressures to conform and can lead to self-censorship or homogenized reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect control via hiring, promotion, and institutional buffering
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if news departments are organizationally buffered, content is still controlled indirectly through hiring and promotion practices and through norms that produce self-censorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanisms: selecting employees who fit organizational values, promoting those who conform, and structuring career incentives produce content alignment with organizational interests. Buffering reduces overt interference but not indirect influences.
